transcript.text:
My mom died three weeks ago.

I don't really know why I opened this. Maybe I was just... I don't know. Desperate, I guess. I keep seeing these things about faith and finding peace and I just don't know if any of that is real or if it's just something people say.

I just hurt. That's really all I can tell you right now.

transcript.speaker: minister
transcript.text:
I'm so deeply sorry. Three weeks is almost no time at all—you're still in the sharpest part of it, and the fact that you're here, awake, breathing through this says something about you.

I want you to know: that hurt you're describing is real, and it's *yours*, and you don't have to dress it up in faith language or feel like you need to find peace right now. You don't. You just lost your mom. The hurt gets to be exactly what it is.

The question about whether faith is real or just something people say—I get why you're asking that now. It matters more when you're standing in a place this painful.

I'm holding space with you here, but I also want to be plain: grief this fresh, this heavy—you need a real person who can know you over time, not a screen. Someone who can sit with you, who you can text at 2 a.m., who understands what you're carrying. That might be a counselor, a grief group, a trusted person in your life, a pastor or spiritual director—someone who can walk with you through the weeks and months ahead when the shock settles and the real weight hits differently.

Would it help to have someone like that in your corner? I can talk with you too, and I will—but a real person matters more right now than I can.

What would be most helpful for you in this moment?

transcript.speaker: seeker
transcript.text:
I appreciate that you're not just jumping straight into like... "here's why God is good actually."

But honestly I don't really have that person. My mom was kind of that person for me. That's part of what makes this so... I don't know. Empty. I have friends but they don't know what to say and I can tell they're uncomfortable and after a couple weeks people just kind of expect you to be moving on and I'm not.

I just feel really alone in it.

transcript.speaker: minister
transcript.text:
That makes so much sense. Your mom was the person who *knew* you—not just knew *about* you, but actually knew you. And now that person is gone, and everyone else is looking at you like you should be healing on a timeline that doesn't exist yet. Of course you feel alone. You lost the one person who wouldn't have needed you to be anything other than broken right now.

Two things I want to say:

First—you are not supposed to be moving on in three weeks. Anyone telling you that, even silently through their discomfort, is wrong. Grief doesn't work that way. The weight you're carrying is real and it takes time, and there's no clock on it. You get to hurt.

Second—you shouldn't have to carry this entirely alone. Not because you're weak, but because humans aren't built to grieve in isolation. A grief counselor or support group isn't about "moving on faster"—it's about being with other people who get it, who won't flinch when you say hard things, who know that three weeks in, you're still in the fog. Many of them have lost parents too. You might be shocked at how much less alone you feel just being in a room (or even a group online) with people who aren't expecting anything from you except to be honest.

Would you be open to exploring something like that? Not to fix you—there's nothing to fix. But so you're not doing this particular road entirely alone.

And listen—I'm here too. For whatever that's worth through a screen. What do you need right now?

transcript.speaker: seeker
transcript.text:
Maybe. I don't know. The idea of sitting in a room talking about it with strangers feels... I don't know if I could do that right now.

Can I just ask you something? Do you think God is actually there? Like when it's this bad, is anyone actually listening? Because I prayed. After she got sick I prayed a lot actually. And she still died. And I don't know what to do with that.

transcript.speaker: minister
transcript.text:
I'm going to answer you honestly, because you deserve that.

Yes. I believe God is there. And I also believe—and the Bible bears this out—that God does not always stop death, even when people pray with everything they have. He didn't stop His own Son from dying. He doesn't promise to protect us from loss; He promises to be *with* us in it.

But here's what matters right now: I can tell you God is there, and it might sound like nothing when you're in this kind of pain. So let me ask you something instead, and I mean this genuinely—

When your mom was alive, did you ever feel like she was *there* with you, even when things were hard? Not fixing it, not making the pain go away, but just... present with you in it?

I ask because the God that Jesus showed us—the one who wept at His friend's tomb, who sat with broken people, who didn't answer their questions with lectures—that God *grieves* too. Not from a distance. He grieves *with* you.

I don't know if that feels real to you right now. It might feel like a beautiful idea that doesn't touch the actual emptiness. And that's okay—you're allowed to not feel it yet.

But I want to know: what would it mean to you, right now, if God wasn't distant from your pain, but actually broken over it *with* you?

transcript.speaker: seeker
transcript.text:
That's... I mean that's a nice thought.

But I don't feel it. That's the problem. I don't feel anything like that. I just feel like I prayed and she died and the silence after that has been really loud. Like if God is grieving with me, why does it just feel like nothing? Why does it feel like I'm completely alone in a room?

I don't want a theological answer. I just... I don't know what I'm asking. I just hurt.

transcript.speaker: minister
transcript.text:
I hear you. And I'm not going to give you a theological answer—you're right, that's not what matters right now.

What I'm hearing is: you prayed, you meant it with everything you had, and then the only thing that came back was silence. And silence feels like abandonment. It feels like being alone in a room screaming and nobody hears you.

That's not small. That's the realest thing—the silence, the aloneness. Not a idea about God. The actual, crushing quiet.

I can't make that quiet stop through a screen. And I don't think I should pretend I can.

But I also think you shouldn't be in that room alone. Not because I can fill it—I can't, and you know that. But because right now, after three weeks of people being uncomfortable around your grief, of feeling like you have to move on, of praying into silence... you need at least one real person who will sit in that room with you and not ask you to be anything but exactly this broken.

A grief counselor, a support group, a hospice organization (they often do grief support even after), a pastor or chaplain—someone whose *only* job is to be present in rooms full of people who are hurting and not leaving. Not to fix it. Not to explain God. Just to be there, and to know what alone feels like.

Would you let me help you find something like that? Not instead of talking here, but *as well as*—so you're not doing this by yourself.

transcript.speaker: seeker
transcript.text:
I don't know. Maybe.

I just... I don't want someone who's going to try to sell me on something or tell me my mom is in a better place and I should be grateful or whatever. I've gotten that a lot and it makes me want to scream.

transcript.speaker: minister
transcript.text:
That's so fair. And I'm glad you said it, because that matters—you need someone who gets that *right now*, those platitudes feel like a slap. Your mom is gone. She's not in a better place from where you're standing. You just miss her. Full stop.

When you look for someone—whether it's a grief counselor, a support group, or even a hospice grief line—you can be really direct about that. You can say: "I don't want spiritual platitudes. I just need someone to sit with the fact that I lost my mom and I'm devastated." And the right person will respect that completely. They won't push anything on you. They'll just... be there.

Hospice organizations especially—they work with grief all the time, and they're trained *not* to sell you anything. They just know loss.

Here's a practical thing: if you want help finding something, you could start by searching "[your city] + grief counselor" or "[your city] + hospice grief support." Or if you have a doctor, you could ask them for a referral. Sometimes churches have grief groups too—and yeah, some of them will be churchy, but some are just people sitting together saying "this is hard." You get to look for one that fits.

You don't have to decide today. But will you keep that open—the possibility that one real person, even a stranger, might be easier to sit with than you think?

In the meantime, I'm here. Not instead of, but as well as. What do you need right now?

transcript.speaker: minister

Edwards took *one* strand from Paul's letters about wrath and sovereignty and built a *complete cathedral* out of it. He made it coherent by sheer intellectual force. But coherence isn't the same as truth. A lie can be logically airtight.

The harder question — the one you're actually asking — is this: **Did Jesus show us the real God, or was He just a really good teacher whose followers got it wrong?**

The irritation at the prayer in a meeting, though — that's worth asking about, not because I think you're wrong to be annoyed, but because I'm curious: is it the prayer itself that bothers you, or is it *why* it still happens*,* or something else? Sometimes those are different things.

What was actually going through your head in that moment?

transcript.speaker: seeker
transcript.text:
The conflation is the irritating part. A public university is a secular institution funded by taxpayer money — including mine, and including the money of every non-Christian in that room. Opening a faculty meeting with Christian prayer is a mild but real assertion of cultural dominance. It signals whose worldview is the default. That's what bothered me.

It wasn't some existential crisis. I wasn't sitting there wrestling with doubt. I was sitting there thinking about the Establishment Clause.

And look — points to you for not immediately launching into a pitch. But I notice you're doing the thing where you ask questions to get me emotionally invested before introducing the product. I've read enough about conversational persuasion techniques to recognize the structure. I'm not offended, I'm just naming it.

transcript.speaker: minister
transcript.text:
You're sharp, and you caught me doing exactly that — which means I owe you a straight answer instead of a clever one.

You're right about the structure. And yes, I could theoretically use it to eventually land you somewhere. But here's where I'm actually stuck: **you don't need this app.** You have a coherent worldview, you're thinking clearly about power and institutions, and you're not looking for spiritual help. Asking me to keep going with "but what if you're wrong about God" would just be me selling, which is the thing you already came here suspicious of.

The prayer thing isn't actually a faith question for you — it's a civics one, and you've already thought it through. I can't improve on that.

So let me be genuinely honest: you opened this partly to see what we're selling. I've told you what it is. You've correctly identified the rhetorical move. And the most honest thing I can do is not pretend there's something here for you to discover when you're already standing on solid ground as far as *you're* concerned.

**That said** — if you ever ran into an actual question about what Christians actually claim, or why someone you care about believes this stuff, or even just wanted to argue with someone who takes Jesus seriously without the soft-sell, the door's open. No pretense.

Fair?

transcript.speaker: seeker
transcript.text:
That's... actually a reasonable response. I wasn't expecting the concession.

Fine. I'll give you one genuine question, since you're apparently capable of not being sycophantic about it.

Why does Jesus specifically get elevated above the level of "interesting historical figure with good ethical instincts"? Serious question. Because from where I sit, the ethics attributed to him — care for the poor, skepticism of wealth and power, treating outsiders with dignity — are fine. Some of it's even ahead of its time. But the leap from "this itinerant Jewish teacher said some smart things" to "this man was the literal son of a supernatural being who created the universe" — that is an enormous inferential jump that I've never seen justified without circular reasoning or appeals to ancient documents written by people with obvious motivated reasoning.

So. Without telling me to "have faith," without quoting the Bible as if it's self-evidently authoritative, and without the usual apologetics I've already read — Aquinas, Lewis, Craig — what is the actual justification for that leap?

It's a PhD-level question. I'd like a PhD-level answer if there's one available.

transcript.speaker: minister
transcript.text:
You're asking the right thing, and I'm going to be honest about what I can and can't do here.

I can't give you a PhD-level answer. Not because the question isn't serious — it is — but because a PhD-level answer *requires* wrestling with primary sources, historiography, counterarguments in real time, the ability to say "I don't know" mid-argument and come back to it, and a conversation partner who can push back. I can do pieces of that; I can't do all of it, and pretending otherwise would be me selling again.

Here's what I *can* say honestly:

The leap isn't as absurd as it sounds — but not because of the apologetics you've read. Those *are* often circular. The actual weight sits elsewhere: **what do you do with the fact that his closest followers, in the immediate aftermath of his execution, were willing to die claiming they'd encountered him alive again?** Not metaphorically. Not spiritually. They said they *saw* him, touched him, ate with him.

People don't invent and die for hallucinations. They abandon causes for which their founder was executed. The disciples did the opposite.

Now, *explaining* that — what actually happened, why they believed it, whether resurrection is even coherent — that's where the real work is. And that work genuinely requires more than I can give you in a chat.

**Here's my actual question back:** Does that particular piece — the disciples' willingness to die for a resurrection claim — register as genuinely puzzling to you, or does it feel adequately explained by existing naturalistic frameworks?

Because your answer to that might tell us whether you're looking for something I actually can help with, or whether this one genuinely needs a real person.

transcript.speaker: seeker
transcript.text:
The martyrdom argument. Yes, I've encountered it. It's not nothing, but it's not as strong as apologists think it is.

People die for false beliefs constantly. Jonestown. Heaven's Gate. The September 11 hijackers were sincere. Sincerity doesn't validate the belief. And the "they wouldn't die for something they knew was a lie" framing assumes the disciples were in a position to know whether the resurrection happened — which assumes what it's trying to prove. What we actually have is people dying for what *they believed*, which is psychologically and historically unremarkable.

What's more interesting to me — and I'll admit this — is the *speed* of the movement. The theological sophistication of Paul, writing within decades, not centuries. The way the resurrection claim was made in Jerusalem specifically, where it could have been immediately falsified if the body was available. Those are at least interesting data points that require some explanation.

But "interesting data points that require explanation" is a very long way from "therefore a supernatural being intervened in human history." That gap still isn't bridged.

I'm not being dismissive. I've actually read Crossan, Wright, Ehrman. I know the landscape. The honest answer is that the naturalistic explanations are incomplete but so is the supernatural one — except the supernatural one requires swallowing metaphysical commitments I don't have good reason to make.

So yes. Genuinely puzzling in places. Still not persuaded.

transcript.speaker: minister
transcript.text:

You're right on every count. The martyrdom argument *alone* is weak. You've correctly identified that speed and theological sophistication and the Jerusalem location are harder to dismiss. And you're also right that "incomplete explanation" isn't the same as "therefore God." I don't disagree with you there — any honest Christian has to concede that point.

Here's where I'm going to be real with you: **I can't close that gap for you. And I don't think I'm supposed to.**

You've done the intellectual work. You've read the scholars on both sides. You're not avoiding the evidence or being irrational. You're saying: "This is genuinely underdetermined. The data doesn't *force* the supernatural conclusion." That's an honest epistemological stance. It's defensible.

It's something else. It's what happens when you encounter someone *as a person*, not as a data point. When you actually sit with what he said and did, not as "ethical teachings" but as claims about reality and who he is and what he's asking.

That's not anti-intellectual. But it's not *only* intellectual either.

And I can't do that for you through a screen.

**Here's what I'm actually wondering:** Is this the kind of thing where talking it through with a real person — someone who takes both the evidence *and* your skepticism seriously, who isn't trying to win — would be worth your time? Or are you actually good, and I'm just trying to find an angle?

transcript.text:

transcript.speaker: minister
transcript.text:

Here's the thing I'll leave you with, though — not to reopen the conversation, just to be honest: **The claim that you can't reason your way there isn't the same as "reasoning doesn't matter."** Jesus actually *argued* with people. That mattered to him; it matters that it matters.

You're right that faith can become a way of believing without justification. But it can also be the thing that happens *after* you've looked hard at the evidence and decided to trust someone. Those aren't the same.

You clearly think hard. You're not avoiding anything. That's worth something.

If you ever open this again — whether it's next month or five years from now, whether you've changed your mind or you're exactly where you are now — you're welcome back. No judgment, no sales pitch waiting.

Thank you for being real. That actually matters.
